name: Grilled Shrimp with Garlic and Lemon
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt frames grilled shrimp as a conflict between two goals: browning needs hard, fast heat, but shrimp go from snappy to rubbery within a few degrees, and they are too small to char before the middle overcooks. His fix is a set of pre-treatments rather than a hotter fire alone. Tossing the shrimp with salt, a little sugar and baking soda helps on three fronts, since salt keeps them holding moisture, sugar speeds surface browning, and the alkaline baking soda both firms the texture and raises pH so the Maillard reaction runs faster. He then packs the shrimp tightly against each other on double skewers, a Cook's Illustrated idea, because less exposed surface slows heat reaching the centers and buys grilling time. Finally he air-dries the skewers uncovered in the fridge for an hour, on the logic that surface moisture must evaporate before browning can start, and dresses the shrimp in a garlic-lemon-parsley oil after cooking rather than marinating beforehand.
comment_digest: The dominant correction is salt: several reviewers found the finished shrimp too salty, one saying they would leave the salt out entirely next time, another reporting it even while using the specified half teaspoon baking soda and kosher salt. One reader raises a plausible cause, that some shrimp are sold pre-brined and may need soaking first, which suggests salting to taste rather than by the recipe. Cooks working with smaller batches or already-cooked shrimp cut the grilling time sharply, one reporting only one to two minutes per side for jumbo shrimp, while another using 12-per-pound shrimp needed a few minutes more than the stated four to five. Reviewers confirm the salt, sugar and baking soda treatment as the part worth keeping. Reported variations that worked: skipping skewers in favor of a grill rack, substituting lime for lemon, and serving over linguine as a grilled scampi.
